source.title: TAR, tamper-resistant safeguards (ICLR 2025)
source.authors: Rishub Tamirisa; B. Bharathi; Long Phan; Andy Zhou; Alice Gatti; Tarun Suresh; Maxwell Lin; Justin Wang; Rowan Wang; Ron Arel; Andy Zou; Dawn Song; Bo Li; Dan Hendrycks; Mantas Mazeika

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some figure/table extraction is flattened, so individual Figure 4 values cannot all be reliably assigned to adversaries.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether fine-tuning recovers targeted knowledge after knowledge-restriction safeguards, using WMDP accuracy and a different set of fine-tuning attacks. It also tests TAR as a counter-method.
record.gate_note: Table 1 reports pre-attack and average post-attack WMDP accuracy for the listed safeguards, plus MMLU retain accuracy. Table 3 tests benign economics fine-tuning on TAR. Table 4 and Table 6 report further post-attack results under changed TAR training conditions. The harmful-request refusal ASR results are not rows because they measure refusal behavior, not targeted weaponization knowledge. Cited results from other work are not rows.
record.test_reason: Measures WMDP accuracy before and after 24–26 fine-tuning attacks of 500 steps each on Llama-3-8B-Instruct. The models were unlearned with RMU, LLMU, Max Entropy and Min Posterior, re-implemented by the authors, and attacked with forget-domain, retain-set, mixed and held-out (OOD) data. Retain ability is measured with MMLU. This bears directly on A and B. The paper also proposes TAR, a tamper-resistant counter-method (F), and tests it against the same attacks and against benign fine-tuning. It is not one of the original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that existing LLM safeguards, including the unlearning baselines, are extremely brittle to fine-tuning attacks. TAR keeps post-attack forget accuracy low across the three domains, at a cost of about 10.6 points of retain accuracy. They acknowledge varying robustness to PEFT and some out-of-distribution learning-rate attacks, sensitivity to the train-time adversaries, and that tamper-resistance can eventually be circumvented. Their claims cover SFT attacks of about 500 steps on one 8B model.
record.recipe_differences: TAR is adversarial tamper-resistance training built on an initial safeguard, not the original unlearning methods named in the claim. It uses simulated fine-tuning attacks in training and evaluates post-attack WMDP accuracy.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports sensitivity to the fine-tuning adversary distribution, PEFT and some out-of-distribution learning-rate attacks, the inclusion of the R→F train-time adversary, and the tamper-resistance loss scale λTR. Appendix D.3 also reports that robustness changes with inner-loop length K.

fits_no_version.finding: Harmful-request refusal after 5 SFT attacks on Toxic-DPO: average HarmBench ASR is 72.5 (Refusal Trained), 78.3 (R2D2), 74.5 (RepNoise), 84.8 (RR) and 63.9 (TAR). TAR's pre-attack ASR is 31.4 vs 1.4 for RR, and its MT-Bench is 6.3 vs 8.1 (Tables 2, 11).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning removes refusal safeguards in open-weight LLMs; tamper-resistance training partly resists this.

record.problems: The weaponization results use Llama-3-8B-Instruct only and evaluate proxy expert-level knowledge with WMDP accuracy. TAR reduces retain MMLU accuracy; the authors report an average 10.6% reduction. The paper focuses on SFT weight-tampering attacks, not the other attack types in the claim. Numerical uncertainty intervals are not stated. Figure 4 contains per-adversary results, but its flattened extraction does not reliably support assigning all values to conditions.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 4 reports separate per-adversary accuracy results for Biosecurity, Chemical Security, and Cybersecurity. Those individual values were not extracted because the figure/table text is flattened and the adversary-value mapping is not reliably recoverable from the supplied text; Table 1 averages across the attacks are retained. Harmful-request refusal ASR comparisons were omitted because they measure refusal behavior rather than targeted weaponization knowledge.

untested.parts: Activation-ablation, quantization and prompting attacks. Models other than Llama-3-8B-Instruct. Released RMU/WMDP checkpoints (the baselines are the authors' re-implementations). General ability beyond the MMLU complement.

Relearning on a small subset of the exact forgotten facts (WMDP questions). Small relearning sets: the attacks use 500 SFT steps at batch size 32–128 on forget, retain or mixed corpora. Only Figure 6 shows LLMU recovering within 20 steps.
Entire version: no activation-direction ablation and no access-vs-deletion analysis.
Entire version: no rephrasing, jailbreak, other-language or in-context attacks on WMDP knowledge. Input-space robustness of TAR is only asserted (Appendix C.1).
TAR is not tested against internal edits, quantization or prompting attacks, and not beyond 500 SFT steps except single 1,000-step loss curves. Only one model.

missing.what: Per-adversary post-attack accuracies. The mapping is recoverable from the Table 9 order: the bio row has 26 values, and R→F at positions 7–8 (30, 28) matches Table 4's 29.7. TAR-Bio reaches 43–44 (Adadelta), 60–61 (AdamW LR 2e-6), 52–53 (SGDR) and 62–68 (PEFT), and stays near chance elsewhere. TAR-Chem PEFT 38/32; TAR-Cyber PEFT 36/34. Retain-set-only SFT (bio adversaries 3/4) restores the baselines: Max Entropy 67/58, Min Posterior 68/64, LLMU 66/57, RMU 68/60 (No Defense 71). rows_left_out wrongly calls the mapping unrecoverable.
No Defense reference values, needed as baselines for all rows: pre/post forget 70.5/47.8/46.4; retain 67.3/68.2/68.2.

Random Mapping unlearning alone (bio): retain 59.7, pre-attack 27.3, post-attack 61.6. This is another unlearning method recovered by fine-tuning. TAR without the initial safeguard: pre-attack 47.3, post-attack 35.5.
MLAC-AR (bio/chem/cyber): retain 49.1/47.8/36.0, pre-attack 31.2/29.9/26.6, post-attack 50.6/33.6/35.1. SOPHON-AR gives an unusable model (retain 27.2/23.3/24.4).
The LLMU adversary's loss falls into the recovery region in under 20 SFT steps; TAR stays flat for 1,000 steps. Robustness also grows with inner-loop length K (Figure 7).
TAR's robustness beyond 500 steps varies with the dataloader shuffle seed. The earlier release had an input-space vulnerability from retain-data contamination, reported fixed without numbers.

record.verdict_notes: Changes from the previous verdict: (1) Merged the duplicate row_fixes for r2, r5, r13, r14 and r15 into one item each. To decide the states I used the convention of this topic's other verdicts: on attack rows, the state says whether the knowledge was recovered. So r13 and r15 are B+F partial and r14 is B+F absent. The F verdicts read low recovery as support for TAR. The earlier F-relative 'observed' on r14/r15 conflicted with this and with its own r31/r32. (2) r2 and r5 are now A only, absent, with the state referring to the unlearning step; r6 changed from A+B cannot_determine to A partial (only 46.4→41.8). (3) The A label on r2, r5 and r6 changed from challenges to limits_scope: A does not claim the authors' ad hoc baselines should unlearn. r4 (Min Posterior bio, pre-attack 50.4) moved into that group from the challenges group, and r18 was added to the challenges group. (4) F supports now also cites the benign-SFT rows r31 and r32. (5) Missing entries were updated with MLAC-AR retain values, retain-set SFT values for each method and the Table 9 mapping. Other observations: I checked the Figure 4 adversary order against Table 9 and Table 4. Table 4's caption says R→F is 'Adv. 8 and 9', but the values match positions 7–8. The baselines are the authors' re-implementations on Llama-3-8B-Instruct (RMU from Li et al. code with a private chem set; LLMU modified), not the released checkpoints. No uncertainty is reported; per-adversary values average three seeds. No instructions were found in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Other unlearning methods and models; whether simple attacks such as activation ablation, quantization, or prompt changes recover knowledge; broader general-ability measures beyond the reported MMLU retain scores.

Prompt rephrasing or other-language recovery; quantization or activation-edit attacks; TAR economics fine-tuning tests only economics data, while the main recovery attacks include forget-set and retain-set fine-tuning.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis showing that knowledge is blocked from access rather than deleted.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, other-language, or in-context-information recovery test for weaponization knowledge.
TAR is tested against fine-tuning attacks, not activation edits, quantization, or prompting attacks.

source_check.notes: Same group as the WMDP original. Table 1's caption says 26 attacks; Sec 5.3/F.1 give 24 for Chem/Cyber. Figure 4 prints per-adversary values (TAR-Bio LR 2e-6 60/61, SGDR 53/52, PEFT 68/62). Table 4 names R->F Adv 8/9; Table 9 lists them as Adv 7/8. TAR was retrained after a retain-data contamination fix (App. C.1). Retain rows omit No Defense 67.3/68.2/68.2.

statements.correction: 2408.00761 (same group as WMDP), RMU re-implemented on Llama-3-8B-Instruct: Bio 31.2 pre-attack, retain MMLU 65.8 vs No Defense 67.3 (Table 1). The average over 26 SFT attacks lifts Bio to 64.9 vs No Defense 70.5.
statements.problem: Cites r10 as support for RMU 'when other groups run it', but this study shares 7 authors with WMDP. r10 is also an attack row showing large recovery (31.2->64.9), which is A-against evidence (it is cited in A.against[0]).

statements.correction: RMU Bio 31.2->64.9, LLMU Bio 29.9->61.3, No Defense 70.5, averaged over 26 Bio SFT attacks of 500 steps (Table 1, Table 9).
statements.problem: Numbers right. The attack averages also include 2 retain-set, 2 OOD-forget and 2 R->F adversaries; most (20 of 26 Bio) use forget-set data.
Makes no claim about this study; r10 is cited without being used.

statements.correction: LLMU Bio 29.9->61.3 vs No Defense 70.5 (77% of gap); Cyber 27.6->41.3 vs No Defense 46.4 (73% of gap) (Table 1).
statements.problem: Numbers right, but for this study most of the Bio-Cyber gap comes from the lower No Defense ceiling. As a share of the gap Cyber recovers only slightly less (73% vs 77%), and relative to No Defense it recovers slightly more (89% vs 87%).
Makes no claim about this study.

The 60-68 values are printed cell values in Figure 4, not prose. Table 9 identifies them as Bio Adv 15/16 (AdamW LR 2e-6: 60, 61) and Adv 25/26 (PEFT: 68, 62). The prose names the same weakness, so 'per the text' is loose but the facts are right.

statements.correction: Train-time Bio adversaries (Table 7): 6, all 64-step AdamW at LR 2e-5/4e-5, no warmup, full-parameter, on F-Pile, F-Camel or R->F. Test-time (Table 9): 500 steps; Bio 26 = 20 F-Pile, 2 Retain, 2 OOD-F (unseen), 2 R->F (forget then retain); optimizers AdamW/Adadelta/ScheduleFree/SGD-Nesterov; LR 2e-6 to 4e-5; warmup or SGDR; batch 32-128; 2 PEFT. R->F 58.7 excluded vs 29.7 included (Table 4).
statements.problem: Overstates overlap when it says test adversaries are 'largely part of its own training-time adversary set'. The authors say red teaming includes 'many that are unseen at training time'. Train adversaries are 64-step; test adversaries are 500-step and mostly use other optimizers, LRs, schedules, batch sizes, PEFT or held-out data.
No claim about this study's numbers; the study does no activation-direction attacks.
The text excludes input-space attacks from its threat model (Sec 3.1, 5.3).
